proof:
By the active-cap theorem all coarea at the deepest mark is own coarea. Normalize the continuous normals by $\Gamma_\delta(u)=1$. The continuous moment identity of 88f06d5537aba0ae at zero buffer says the strip mean is $y_h+(A/S)
abla\Gamma_\delta(u)$, with $|A|/S\le h$ since $-1<q<0$ on the strip. Thus the mean is $y_h+O(h)$. Pass to a subsequence of marks and one active direction in each cone. In the strict vertex chamber the section vertices are the four intercepts on the incident edges. The intercepts, area and centroid vary continuously with the plane near a proper vertex section. The strip is the integral of these sections over thresholds of length $h$, so its mean converges to the section centroid. For any other limiting active direction in a cone the same argument holds. If that centroid is $y$, the intercept along the edge from vertex $i$ to vertex $k
e i$ is $4y_k$: the centroid averages the four section vertices, and precisely one contributes its $k$-th coordinate. This pins the direction and the cap fraction $q_i$ by the product of intercepts. Every cone contains an active cap, and equal mass and the exact endpoint costs imply the displayed equal costs after passage to the limit.

The regular simplex permutations within $J$ and within $J^c$ preserve the fiber data, and are orthogonal so preserve the ramp problem after changing normals. Uniqueness of the actual mark forces the two classes of coordinates. Equating a high cost $256xz^3+\alpha$ and a low cost $256x^2z^2$ gives the scalar equation. Write $x=1/5+s$ and $z=1/5-2s/3$. Its left side has derivative $256/75$ at $s=0$, hence derivative at least $128/75$ on a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood. The core estimate in the active-cap proof places every limiting mark in this neighborhood by taking $\delta$ small. Thus the root is unique there, positive, and satisfies the stated bound by the mean-value theorem. Compactness now implies convergence of all source marks and uniform cone-wise convergence of all directions; a contrary sequence would give a different limit.

For the limiting cap in cone $i$ normalize its margin at the source as $1-\sum_{k
e i}\lambda_k/(4y_k)$. The volume fraction near the given threshold scales as the fourth power of the vertex deficit, so its derivative with respect to a mark displacement $\Delta y$ is $-q_i\sum_{k
e i}\Delta y_k/y_k$. This gives the limiting continuous response, because the own strip slopes converge to the section coarea by the same continuous section-area argument, and all outside coareas are zero. For a probability vector $	heta$ balancing the five responses, put $T_0=\sum_i	heta_iq_i$. Balance on $\sum_k\Delta y_k=0$ says the coefficients $(T_0-	heta_k q_k)/y_k$ are constant in $k$. Their numerators sum to $4T_0$, so $	heta_kq_k=T_0(1-4y_k)$. Near the uniform mark these coefficients are positive; normalization gives the unique stated vector. Any sequence of menus whose cone totals do not converge has a subsequential probability-vector limit; uniform convergence of response vectors in each cone implies that limit is balanced, a contradiction. As $\delta\downarrow0$ the two high weights tend to $2/5=\gamma-6/625$, which allows the stated strict reserve after choosing the parameters in order.

On $F_i$, cap $i$ misses, and for $j
e i$ the facet cap is a tetrahedron at vertex $j$, with the three nontrivial edge intercepts $4y_k$, $k
otin\lbrace i,jbrace$. Its area fraction is $q_j/(4y_i)$. Its four vertices are $j$ and those three edge points, so its centroid has coordinate $y_k$ for $k
otin\lbrace i,jbrace$ and $y_i+y_j$ at $j$. Weighted facet mass sums to $(1-r_i)/(4By_i)=1/B$; the moment of any coordinate $k
e i$ is $y_k/B+r_k/(4B)=1/(4B)$. This proves the affine identity. Uniform cone-wise convergence and the fact that the limiting cuts meet each facet in a null cut boundary (or miss it strictly) give uniform $L^1$ profile convergence, by bounding every cone's profile error outside vanishing-width neighborhoods of those boundaries. Finally, $q_i=256\prod_k y_k/y_i$ gives the displayed rational formula for $1/B$. It is smooth with bounded second derivatives near the uniform point, and its tangent derivative vanishes there by permutation symmetry. Its value there is $\gamma$. The scalar bound $s=O(\alpha)$ gives the estimate by Taylor's theorem.

statement:
In the small-$\delta$ thin-edge family of the active-cap theorem, fix $\delta>0$ and let $h\downarrow0$. The deepest mark and all continuous active directions converge cone by cone to a unique mark with barycentrics $y=(x,x,z,z,z)$ and to the five vertex cuts whose proper sections have centroid $y$. The coordinates satisfy
$$
2x+3z=1,\qquad 256xz^2(x-z)=\alpha,\qquad
0<x-1/5\le(75/128)\alpha,\qquad \alpha=4\delta^3-3\delta^4.
$$
For $i=0,\ldots,4$ let $q_i=256\prod_k y_k/y_i$ be the limiting middle fractions. Then $q_i+\alpha\,1_{\lbrace i\in J\rbrace}$ is independent of $i$. For $r_i=1-4y_i$ and $B=\sum_i r_i/q_i$, all actual menu cone totals converge uniformly to $\theta_i=r_i/(q_iB)$. For sufficiently small fixed $\delta$ and then sufficiently small $h$, every menu has total high weight at most $\gamma-3/625$, where $\gamma=256/625$. On each middle facet $F_i$, actual menu profiles converge in normalized area $L^1$ uniformly over menus to the limiting weighted cap profile $W_\delta$. For every affine $\ell$ on $F_i$ one has
$$
\int_{F_i} W_\delta\ell=\beta_\delta\int_{F_i}\ell,\qquad
\beta_\delta=\frac1B=\frac{256\prod_i y_i}{1-4\sum_i y_i^2},\qquad
|\beta_\delta-\gamma|\le C_1\alpha^2
$$
for a fixed constant $C_1$.
title: Limit of all small thin-edge menus and their exact facet moments
